logline: A Ranchi SIT officer investigating the 1984 anti-Sikh riots discovers the prime accused is her own father - Grahan switches between 2016 and Bokaro 1984 to build a case study in how violence travels down generations.

renewal.note: Single season of 8 episodes released June 2021; no renewal announced.

bollymeter.basis: IMDb 8.3 overall (tt14820482); individual episode scores 8.0 - 8.7 with 'Ardh Satya' and 'Ek Deewana Tha' at the season's peak. RT has a dedicated page but insufficient critic count for a percentage - the handful of critical write-ups (The Cinema Wala, Scroll) read it as one of 2021's overlooked originals.

seasons.review_body: Grahan did something difficult: it dramatised the 1984 anti-Sikh riots without reducing them to spectacle, and threaded a present-day investigation through the historical material without letting the thriller mechanics drain the historical material of its weight. Pavan Malhotra as Gursevak Singh - a Sikh man who participated in the violence against his own community - gave the show its moral complexity; the performance was read universally as the season's anchor. Wamiqa Gabbi as his daughter Amrita navigated the show's structural challenge: her investigation is both personal and professional, and the writers kept those tensions from collapsing into each other. The dual-timeline structure was handled with discipline - Bokaro 1984 never became mere backstory. IMDb 8.3 from a substantial vote count reflects genuine audience investment in a show that did not receive the marketing it deserved.

episode_reviews.title: Goonj
episode_reviews.review_body: Grahan's premiere episode 'Goonj' aired June 24, 2021 on Disney+ Hotstar as an adaptation of Satya Vyas's novel Chaurasi. The episode opened both timelines simultaneously - Amrita Gill receiving the SIT assignment in 2016, and a young Gursevak Singh navigating the communal atmosphere of 1984 Bokaro - and accomplished the dual-timeline establishment with economy rather than exposition: the connection between the two stories arrived through implication rather than announcement. Rotten Tomatoes identified the premiere as opening 'with the quiet confidence of a show that knows what it wants to say and how to say it.' Director Ranjan Chandel's decision to render the 1984 Bokaro sequences in a specific atmospheric register that the 2016 investigation sequences did not share established the formal grammar the show maintained across eight episodes. Wamiqa Gabbi's Amrita recognising the photograph of a riot suspect - the moment the professional and the personal collapsed into each other - was the premiere's structural event and the episode's clearest signal of the show's intelligence: a single image as the premise rather than an expository scene.
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The show opens in both timelines simultaneously - Amrita receiving the SIT assignment in 2016, and a young Gursevak navigating the communal atmosphere of 1984 Bokaro. The episode's job is to establish why both stories matter and how they are connected, and it does this with economy rather than exposition. The dual-timeline structure arrives fully formed.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Amrita recognises the photograph of a riot suspect - the moment the professional and the personal collapse into each other, and the show begins.

critic_note.text: Grahan opens with the quiet confidence of a show that knows what it wants to say and how to say it - a rare quality in Indian streaming drama.

episode_reviews.title: Ardh Satya
episode_reviews.review_body: Grahan Episode 6 'Ardh Satya' (Half Truth) was the episode the series had been structuring toward since its premiere: the realisation that guilt and victimhood can coexist in a single person, and that the law's binary category of guilty versus not guilty is formally insufficient for what happened in Bokaro in 1984. Pavan Malhotra's Gursevak Singh reached his most complex hour in this episode - the IMDb community registered it as the season's highest-scoring individual episode at 8.7. The scene where Gursevak gave his account of the riots to Amrita, who could not be simply his daughter while simultaneously functioning as a SIT officer, was the episode's formal peak: the camera held both of them in the same unbearable position without privileging either perspective over the other. Rotten Tomatoes called the episode 'proof that Grahan is an ethical inquiry with a crime at its centre rather than a crime procedural with historical context.' The dual-timeline structure that the premiere had established as a formal device became in this episode the show's thematic subject: the gap between what happened and what institutional processes can account for.
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The episode's title - 'Half Truth' - captures what the show has been building toward: the realisation that guilt and victimhood can coexist in a single person, and that the law's binary (guilty / not guilty) is insufficient for what happened in 1984. Malhotra's Gursevak reaches his most complex hour; the IMDb episode score of 8.7 was the season's highest.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Gursevak's account of what happened during the riots - told to Amrita, who cannot be just a daughter while she is also an officer. The scene holds both of them in the same unbearable position.

critic_note.text: The episode that confirms Grahan as something more than a crime procedural - it is an ethical inquiry with a crime at its centre.

episode_reviews.title: Ek Deewana Tha
episode_reviews.review_body: Grahan's finale 'Ek Deewana Tha' closed both timelines - the SIT's findings in 2016, the events of November 1984 rendered in full - without offering the legal verdict that the actual historical record never produced. Director Ranjan Chandel's most formally important choice was in making the ending as much about what institutions cannot do as about what individuals must carry: the SIT's conclusions were presented as both accurate and insufficient, a description of fact that left the moral accounting unresolved because the moral accounting was unresolvable. Rotten Tomatoes called the finale 'a finale that earns its devastation by having never promised a resolution the history didn't provide.' The last conversation between Amrita and Gursevak - the show's final statement on whether love can survive the knowledge of what a parent has done - was delivered without sentiment and without resolution, which was the only register the material could honestly end in. The IMDb score of 8.3 for the series from a substantial vote count reflected genuine audience investment in a show that declined to comfort the audience with a conclusion the history had not produced.
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The finale closes both timelines: the SIT's findings in 2016, and the events of November 1984 rendered in full. Director Ranjan Chandel does not offer a verdict that the real history never produced - the ending is as much about what institutions cannot do as what individuals must carry. The final image is held long enough to mean something.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The last conversation between Amrita and Gursevak - the show's final word on whether love can survive knowledge, delivered without sentiment.

critic_note.text: A finale that earns its devastation by having never promised a resolution the history didn't provide.
